 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

 [2026] IESC 9 

 Record No.: 2024/75 

 Dunne J. 

 Woulfe J. 

 Murray J. 

 Collins J. 

 Donnelly J. 

   

 Between: 

 ACE AUTOBODY LIMITED 

 Plaintiff/Respondent 

 -and- 

 MOTORPARK LIMITED, BRECOL LIMITED AND JDM AUTOMOTIVE LIMITED 

 Defendants/Appellants 

   

 

 

 JUDGMENT of Mr. Justice Woulfe delivered on the 18 th day of February, 2026 

   

 Introduction 

 1.       I have had the benefit of reading a draft of the judgment which Collins J. proposes to deliver herein, and I am happy to gratefully adopt the comprehensive account of the facts, and also the comprehensive account of the proceedings in the Courts below, contained in his judgment. 

 2.       I agree with the summary of the three issues arising in this appeal as set out by Collins J. at para. 50 of his judgment. 

 3.       As regards the first issue, I agree with the conclusion arrived at by Collins J. that there was no concluded agreement to grant a ten year lease of the Body Shop to the plaintiff, Ace Autobody Limited ("Ace"). 

 4.       As regards the second issue, as to whether, if there was such an agreement, it was enforceable by reason of part performance, I again agree with the conclusion of Collins J. that this issue does not arise, in the absence of a concluded agreement. 

 Proprietary Estoppel 

 5.       Where respectfully I part company to some extent with the majority of the Court, however, is when it comes to the third issue , i.e. whether, in the absence of an enforceable agreement to grant a lease of the Body Shop, Ace should nonetheless be granted such a lease (or, in the alternative, some other form of remedy or redress) on the basis of proprietary estoppel.  

 6.       While I broadly agree with the principles governing proprietary estoppel as set out by Collins J. in his judgment, I disagree in part with the application of those principles to the facts of the present case.  

 7.       As regards the applicable principles, I note how Biehler and Gavin, Equity and the Law of Trusts in Ireland (8 th ed., 2025) refers (at pp. 1058-1059) to the identification by Lord Walker in Thorner v. Major [2009] 1 WLR 776 of the three main elements of proprietary estoppel as "a representation or assurance made to the claimant; reliance on it by the claimant; and detriment to the claimant in consequence of his (reasonable) reliance".  I note also how the authors emphasise (at p. 1085) the importance of context (to which I will return below), and the fact-sensitive nature of the inquiry.  

 The Representations and Assurances 

 8.       I would apply the relevant principles to the facts of the present case as follows.  Firstly, as regards the first element, in my opinion the Court of Appeal was entitled to find that the first defendant, Motorpark Limited ("Motorpark"), had made sufficiently strong representations or assurances so as to give rise to a proprietary estoppel.  

 9.       At para. 100 of her judgment for the Court below, Whelan J. referred to the clear evidence of Mr. Robin Sutton, the General Manager of Ace, regarding his telephone conversation with Mr. Michael Barry, the Managing Director of Motorpark, on the morning of the 16 th December, 2016 (Day 2, page 43, line 28): 

 "...but the core of it was us moving in and I did bring up with Michael at this stage that the lease wasn't signed and Michael's angle or his approach to the lease was...I can't tell you exact words, but if I was to say it was very much 'We'll get that sorted out, that's all agreed.  We'll just get that sorted out, let's move on'...the lease was just almost something that was going to happen when it happened, that it shouldn't be anything that would be delaying us moving in was very much the message that I was receiving from him, very much, you know, 'That's all agreed, move on'." 

 10.   As Whelan J. noted, and crucially in my opinion, Mr. Sutton was not challenged in cross-examination on this issue.  I agree with Whelan J. that it is very significant that Mr. Michael Barry in his evidence did not effectively either dispute or contradict this evidence, including the characterisation of the import and tenor of words spoken and statements made by him in the course of the phone call of the 16 th December, 2016. 

 11.   Whelan J. noted (at para. 103) how similar representations and assurances had been made and given to Mr. Sutton on the 22 nd December, 2016, by Mr. Michael Barry's son, Mr. Colin Barry, the Motorpark Group General Manager and Company Director: 

 "The evidence of Mr. Sutton (and, significantly not the subject of cross-examination) was that on the 22 nd December, 2016, Mr. Colin Barry had stated: 'We will have it all sorted out for the 12 th ', 'We will have that done by the 12 th ', 'Let's just set the date and move in...that's all done' and elsewhere 'We will do our best to have that done by the 12 th and you will move in on the 16 th '." 

 12.   I agree with the Court below that, contrary to the views of the trial judge, the assurances were clear, unambiguous and not "vague".  In my opinion the assurances could only have suggested, and could only have been reasonably understood by Ace, as meaning that a ten-year lease would be granted, and would be granted on the basis of the letter from the solicitors for Ace to the solicitors for Motorpark dated the 14 th December, 2016.  That letter had set out a number of requests for suggested amendments to the draft lease.  That letter was not replied to by Motorpark's solicitor, because of instructions given by Mr. Michael Barry not to respond, and instead assurances were given directly by the Barrys to Mr. Sutton that everything was agreed, in order to induce Ace to go into possession at the earliest possible date.  

 13.   I turn now to the issue of context, as mentioned earlier.  I would not accept that there is any general rule that proprietary estoppel cannot, in principle, operate in a commercial context.  While certainty and predictability in commercial transactions are of course important interests, in my opinion honest and fair dealing in commercial transactions is an even more important interest, and equitable principles, including proprietary estoppel, are capable in principle of providing a remedy in cases where the overall context demonstrates that there has been highly unconscionable conduct by one party, even if no contract was ultimately concluded. 

 14.   In the present case, in my opinion, the overall context in which the representations and assurances were made or given is highly significant.  As of the 13 th December, 2013, Mr. Michael Barry instructed Motorpark's solicitors not to carry out any further work for the time being in relation to the lease to Ace, and indicated that it might be that the transaction would not proceed, due to the possibility of an entirely different direction for the Motorpark business. While a later telephone attendance dated the 16 th December, 2016, recorded Mr. Barry as stating that he would proceed with the transaction to Ace, and that Colin Barry would deal with the matter in his absence, that dealing involved the false representations and assurances set out above and the lease was never brought to fruition. 

 15.   A further important aspect of the overall context which arose was that Motorpark was anxious to divest itself of the body repair unit of its business, and to transfer four employees and the cost of same over to Ace.  In my opinion the overall context demonstrates that the conduct of Motorpark was highly unconscionable, and I cannot accept that the doctrine of proprietary estoppel is incapable of providing a remedy for such conduct. 

 16.   In his judgment Collins J. states (at para. 155) that he cannot identify any basis on which the findings of the trial judge in this regard, particularly his characterisation of the assurances made by Motorpark to Ace as "vague assurances", might properly be set aside, consistent with the well-established principles in Hay v. O'Grady [1992] 1 I.R. 210.  With respect, I do not think that Hay v. O'Grady is applicable in this scenario.  The characterisation of the assurances (the content of which was unchallenged) was not a finding of primary fact.  Nor was it an inference of fact which depended upon oral evidence or recollection of facts.  In the circumstances the appellate court was in as good a position as the trial judge to draw the appropriate inference when it came to characterisation of the assurances.  

 Reliance and Detriment 

 17.   As regards the second element of proprietary estoppel, I agree with the Court below (at para. 204) that the evidence of Ace's reliance on the strength of the assurances given was overwhelming.  As noted by Whelan J., the trial judge accepted the evidence of Mr. Sutton and Mr. Plunkett (the General Manager of Ace) that the issue of the lease was continuously raised, including by Mr. Plunkett directly with Mr. Michael Barry on the 17 th January, 2017, and that repeated assurances were given that the lease was forthcoming.  No impediment to the grant of the proposed lease was ever divulged. 

 18.   As regards the third element of proprietary estoppel, the trial judge was clearly entitled to find that Ace had acted to its detriment in undertaking the "substantial" expenditure that it did in the Body Shop, as well as taking on the four employees previously employed by Motorpark.  

 Remedy 

 19.   While I therefore disagree with Collins J. as regards the applicability of the doctrine of proprietary estoppel in the present case, I agree with him that a significant issue would arise as to the appropriate remedy in the overall circumstances.  I also agree that in circumstances where it was unconscionable for Motorpark to allow Ace to undertake the substantial expenditure which it did, a monetary award reflecting that expenditure would adequately remedy such unconscionability.  

 20.   As noted by Collins J., any monetary award to Ace would have to reflect the fact that it has at this stage been in occupation of the Body Shop for nine years, because of the efflux of time pending the final determination of this litigation, and furthermore it is prima facie entitled to a new tenancy under the Landlord and Tenant (Amendment) Act, 1980.  In circumstances where Ace has now had nine years to recover the investment costs of establishing the new Ace business on the premises in question, I agree that the strong likelihood is that it has by now fully recovered its investment costs.  

 21.   In the circumstances, I do not believe it is necessary to remit the matter to the High Court to assess a monetary award for the detriment suffered by Ace.
